d: Full mock interview: design a rate limiter
goal: Your win today: given 'Design a rate limiter', you can run the full 4-step interview — scope with the right questions, sketch the middleware + Redis design, choose and defend an algorithm, survive the distributed and failure curveballs, and close with hard/soft limits, layers and client best practices.
bookSections: Whole chapter via the book's 4-step framework: Step 1 scoping and requirements; Step 2 placement, algorithms, high-level architecture; Step 3 rules, headers, detailed design, distributed environment, performance, monitoring; Step 4 wrap-up (hard vs soft, OSI layers, client best practices)

stages.title: Scope it
stages.teaches: Book framework: Step 1 scope (3–10 min), Step 2 high-level design and buy-in (10–15), Step 3 deep dive (10–25), Step 4 wrap-up (3–5). For this prompt the right questions are: client- or server-side? throttle by IP / user ID / other? scale? distributed? separate service or app code? inform throttled users? — producing the six requirements (accurate limiting, low latency, little memory, distributed, clear exceptions, high fault tolerance).
stages.interaction: Same mechanic as 0008 stage 1: a 45-minute game clock bar, a chat with the interviewer ('Design a rate limiter.'), the 4-step framework strip, a requirements board with 6 slots, and a deck of ~10 question cards (6 good, 4 time-wasters such as 'Which database should the API use for products?', 'How many engineers will maintain it?', 'Should the 429 page have a logo?', 'Do we need machine learning to detect bots?'). Good questions cost 1 minute and earn signal; time-wasters cost 3 minutes and signal. Stage clears when all 6 requirements are pinned. Reveal a caveat callout afterwards: the book skips back-of-the-envelope numbers for this chapter, but an interviewer may ask (e.g. 10M daily users × a few counters × ~ tens of bytes per key ≈ a few hundred MB to low GB in Redis — show the rough maths).
stages.check: All 6 requirements pinned; signal score shown.

stages.title: Sketch it
stages.sub: Step 2 · high-level design and buy-in (10–15 min)
stages.teaches: High-level: client → rate limiter middleware (or API gateway) → API servers; counters in Redis using INCR/EXPIRE; over-limit → 429.
stages.interaction: Whiteboard builder like 0008 stage 2: SVG canvas; tiles Client, Rate limiter middleware, Redis, API servers (+2 distractors: 'Limiter inside the mobile app', 'Counters in MySQL'). Tapping in dependency order draws boxes and arrows; out-of-order costs a minute, a distractor costs a heart with explanation. Then an interviewer prompt in chat: 'Which algorithm?' — learner picks from the five algorithms and one of three justifications; any algorithm with a correct matching justification is accepted (e.g. token bucket + 'allows short bursts, memory efficient, used by Stripe/Amazon'; sliding window counter + 'smooths edges with two counters per key'); a mismatched justification costs signal. Then a predict quiz: 'Limit 2/s, client sends 3 in one second: what does the third get?' → 429.
stages.check: Diagram complete; algorithm + justification picked; quiz answered.

stages.title: Deep dive: the full design
stages.sub: Step 3 · rules, headers, and the detailed diagram
stages.teaches: Detailed design: rules on disk → workers → cache; middleware loads rules from cache and counters/timestamps from Redis; allowed → API servers; limited → 429 + headers (X-Ratelimit-Limit, X-Ratelimit-Remaining, X-Ratelimit-Retry-After), request dropped or sent to a message queue.
stages.interaction: Extend the stage-2 diagram: the interviewer asks 'Where do the rules live, and how does the client know it's throttled?' Learner adds tiles Rules (disk), Workers, Cache, Message queue in a valid order, and then fills a 429 response card: status + three header names chosen from 6 options (3 distractors such as 'X-Server-Load', 'X-Cache-Hit', 'Retry-Never'). Finally a technique map like 0008 stage 3: goals on the left (allow bursts, exact rolling limit, low memory per key, atomic increment, shared count across servers, low latency far away, survive Redis outage) → learner taps the technique (token bucket, sliding window log, sliding window counter, Lua script/sorted set, central Redis, edge servers + eventual consistency, fail open + alerts).
stages.check: Diagram extended; headers correct; technique map complete.

stages.title: Boss: the curveball barrage
stages.teaches: Mixed follow-ups from every quest of the chapter.
stages.interaction: Curveball barrage like 0008 stage 4: 9 rapid scenario cards, 3 choices each; right = 1.5 game-minutes, wrong = heart + extra minute. Cards: fixed-window edge exploit (→ sliding window counter/log); race condition two threads read 3 (→ Lua script); limiters disagree (→ central Redis, not sticky sessions); Redis down (→ fail open with alerts, or fail closed for login); users far away see added latency (→ edge + eventual consistency); flash sale throttles real buyers (→ token bucket / relax rules via monitoring); office behind one NAT IP (→ key by user/API key); key without TTL locks user out (→ atomic INCR+EXPIRE); burst of old requests starving new ones (→ that's leaking bucket; switch or shrink queue).
stages.check: Barrage completed with at least one heart left (engine rules).

stages.title: Wrap it up
stages.teaches: Book's wrap-up talking points: hard vs soft rate limiting (hard: never exceed the threshold; soft: may exceed briefly); rate limiting at different levels — this design is application level (HTTP, OSI layer 7), but you can limit by IP with iptables at layer 3; avoid being rate limited as a client — client cache, know the limit, catch errors and recover gracefully, enough back-off in retries. Also good closers: recap the design and its bottlenecks (Redis as single point of failure, approximate global limits).
stages.interaction: Like 0008 stage 5: 7 closing-move cards; the learner picks exactly 3 and presses 'Deliver my close'. Good cards: 'Hard vs soft limits and which this is', 'Layer 7 here, layer 3 with iptables for floods', 'Client best practices: cache, back off with jitter, handle 429', 'Name the bottleneck: Redis — shard it, add replicas, decide fail-open'. Weak cards: 'Say: I think we're done', 'Re-explain the token bucket from scratch', 'Propose rewriting it in a new language'. Score depends on how many strong cards are picked; interviewer chat reacts to each.
stages.check: Close delivered with at least 2 strong moves.

stages.title: Say it like a senior
stages.interaction: Q.drill. Prompt: 'In 60 seconds: design a rate limiter.' Model answer: scope (server-side, flexible rules by user/IP, distributed, inform users, fault tolerant); middleware or API gateway in front of API servers; algorithm choice with trade-off (token bucket for bursts or sliding window counter for smooth, cheap accuracy); counters in Redis with atomic INCR/EXPIRE or Lua; rules in config files cached by workers; 429 + rate-limit headers, drop or queue; distributed: atomic ops for races, central Redis for sync, edge + eventual consistency for latency; monitor and tune; fail open on cache outage. Checks: scoping; placement; algorithm + trade-off; Redis + atomicity; 429/headers; one distributed issue; one failure mode. Then a scorecard (minutes used, signal, hearts) saved under its own localStorage key (e.g. 'sdq:v1:ch4-boss-interview'), mirroring 0008's separate key.

caveats: The minute ranges are the book's suggestion for a roughly 45-minute session; real loops vary.
The book's rate limiter chapter has no back-of-the-envelope estimation; be ready to do rough Redis memory and QPS maths if asked.
There is no single right algorithm. Interviewers reward a choice tied to a stated requirement (bursts allowed? exactness needed? memory budget?), not a particular name.
The X-Ratelimit-* header names are a convention, not a standard (see 4.4).
